newsitem.title: THAILAND: FEATURE-Khmer Rouge commander said major Thai investor.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Khmer Rouge commander said major Thai investor.

text.p: Ta Mok, the one-legged Khmer Rouge commander regarded by the outside world as a cruel tyrant, is seen by many in this northeastern Thai town as a kind man who helps the poor and is a major investor in the area.

The elusive Ta Mok, who earned the nickname "the butcher" for his cruelty during the 1975-79 Khmer Rouge reign of terror in Cambodia, has never been seen in public. But for residents of the border district of Khu Khan, he is no stranger.
"He is a son of Khu Khan, he belongs here," one local official told Reuters.
"He has contributed a lot to the economy of this province," said another local resident, who claimed to have met Ta Mok last year.
Ta Mok's headquarters is at Anlong Veng, about 15 km (10 miles) across the border in northern Cambodia. It was there in mid June that the Khmer Rouge leadership had a bloody falling out.
Khmer Rouge defence chief Son Sen and almost a dozen members of his family were slaughtered, and Khmer Rouge leader Pol Pot was captured and detained by his own men.
Ta Mok's role in the recent break up of the group's top leaders is still not clear, but few doubt he is still the military strongman in his Anlong Veng fiefdom.
But for people on the Thai side of the border, Ta Mok means business -- not politics.

One Thai resident said he had evidence that Ta Mok and Pol Pot have been investing large sums of money in various businesses, including petrol stations, the construction industry and a department store.
The Khmer Rouge money, which is thought to be largely income derived from logging deals, is invested through proxies, he said.

"There are three groups of people doing business in this town on behalf of Ta Mok and Pol Pot," said one resident. "They have invested several billion baht here (tens of millions of dollars) under the names of their proxies".
Even though local officials may suspect which businessmen are Khmer Rouge proxies, anyone attempting to investigate is warned off by superiors, locals said.

"For example, there was a man who used to earn his living selling clothes, but a few years ago he got involved with the Khmer Rouge in Anlong Veng. He became a millionaire. He owns a petrol station, a construction company and operates dozens of heavy trucks," one local resident said.

Despite his reputation in Cambodia, in the border district of Khu Khan, Ta Mok -- who lost a leg to a landmine in the 1980s -- is known as a kind old man who has on occasion given cattle to poor villagers.
One local politician said Ta Mok gave him rice for distribution to villagers just before an election.
"He is a kind man who never says no when people ask for help," a resident said.
But the president of the Si Sa Ket chamber of commerce, Chaval Mahasuvirachai, played down talk that Ta Mok was a big player in the local economy.
"There are a lot of rumours and speculation about Ta Mok investing here, but I don't think they are true," Chaval told Reuters.

But one source who has been monitoring the movements of the Khmer Rouge for years said he believed Ta Mok and Pol Pot were transferring their wealth to Thailand in anticipation of the end of their Maoist guerrilla group.

Cambodia's First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh is negotiating the defection to the government of less-tainted Khmer Rouge leaders. But he has made it clear that there is no room for either Ta Mok or Pol Pot in any amnesty deal.
